record.title: Discrete chord derivative and minimizer variation inequality

aligned_passages.text:
The full-support manuscript proves that an admissible integrable minimizer
of the zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has Stieltjes support equal to every overlap
scale in [0,1). The proof turns a hypothetical support gap into a constant
interval for the order parameter. Variational contact at the ends of that
interval conflicts with a strict curvature inequality inside it. Along the
auxiliary diffusion, the spatial gradient of the value function is a bounded
martingale. Full support makes this martingale's second moment equal to time;
its terminal correlation with Brownian motion gives the ground-state value.
The manuscript's further argument gives a smooth Stieltjes density, strictly
positive on $(0,1)$, and no atom at zero. Sections 9.1–9.2 derive this stronger
ordinary conclusion separately from the selected formal support statement.

This record reconstructs those arguments and follows the finite Gaussian
approximation into the separate QAOA manuscript. The latter claims that
finite deterministic circuits approach the SK optimum when system size tends
to infinity before circuit depth increases. Its circuit construction needs
additional approximation, synthesis, seed-removal and transfer arguments.
The two formal statements concern full support and scalar value
consequences; neither states QAOA circuit convergence. Their verification
scope is described at the end. See [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main] and
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

Write $u=\Phi_x$, $a=\Phi_{xx}$, and
$dX_t=\gamma(t)u(t,X_t)\,dt+dB_t$, $X_0=0$.
Write $q(t)=\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2]$ for the second moment of this
gradient along $X$.
The first result assumes an admissible minimizer. It constructs its
Stieltjes measure and an associated diffusion, proves
$\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1)$ and strict increase of $\gamma$,
and obtains $\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2=t$ and
$\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$ for every associated diffusion. The selected
formal statement has exactly this conditional scope; it does not assert a
smooth density.
Its [Lean implementation at the fixed source revision][support-main] implements the
[separately stated formal challenge][support-type]. The
[Comparator configuration][support-config] identifies the intended
comparison; the evidence retained with this draft does not establish
a successful research-target replay.

The second result concerns the scalar value. A bounded martingale ends
at a spin-valued random variable whose Brownian correlation represents
$P_*$. Finite Gaussian coefficients approximate that correlation at each
fixed $T<1$, followed by $T\uparrow1$. Its formal statement is separate
and retains the minimizer and diffusion hypotheses where needed. The QAOA
theorem goes further: for each requested accuracy it selects one finite
deterministic circuit, independent of size and disorder, whose limiting
expected energy approaches $P_*$. Neither formal statement asserts that
circuit conclusion.
The scalar clauses are in a [separate Lean implementation][value-main], with their
own [formal challenge][value-type] and [Comparator configuration][value-config].
Those links identify the selected statements, not a completed replay
receipt for either research target.

### 2.5 Order of approximation

The same symbol for a small error must not conceal changing background
objects. The following account fixes those objects before the indicated
limit. A single admissible minimiser and its associated diffusion are
retained throughout the scalar construction.

**Compact-strip regularity.** Fix a derivative order $k\ge1$, a cutoff
$T<1$ and a common coefficient $L^1$ bound. Coefficients converge in $L^1$
within that bound; spatial derivatives converge uniformly on the strip.

**Shape inequalities on a plateau.** Fix the height $c>0$ and a closed
interior neighbourhood. Choose step coefficients equal to $c$ there and
smooth terminal values with $M_m\ge\|\gamma_m\|_\infty$ and
$M_m\to\infty$. The coefficient and terminal approximations may be
chosen as one compatible sequence.

**First variation.** Fix $\gamma$, a feasible $\eta\in L^1$ and initially
$\epsilon>0$. Remove the terminal cutoff before letting
$\epsilon\downarrow0$. The terminal remainder divided by $\epsilon$ is
bounded by an $L^1$ tail of $\eta$.

**Terminal value.** Keep the chosen minimiser and diffusion fixed. Bounded
martingale convergence and integrability of $\gamma$ justify
$t\uparrow1$; no terminal derivative bound is needed.

**Finite Gaussian coefficients.** Fix $\gamma,X$ and $T<1$. Refine $N$
using the fixed-strip bounds, then control the remaining value tail by $1-T$.

For the plateau transfer, tail estimates for a fixed approximant may depend
on that approximant. The passage to the limit uses the integrated
polynomial in the scaled second, third and fourth spatial derivatives of
the value function and the common strip bounds; it does not require
uniform bounds on the auxiliary density scores. Sections 3 and 4 explain
the variation and plateau-transfer arguments, and §7 gives a complete scalar error
budget. The further choices used to produce a circuit appear in §8.6.
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1, Lemma 6.1, Proposition 5.1 and
Proposition 7.2][fs-main].

**Proposition 3.1 (variational contact).** For an admissible minimizer, the potential $G(s)=\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt$ is nonnegative on $[0,1)$ and vanishes on $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma$. At every $s\in S$, $q(s)=s$ and $q'(s)\le1$, with a right derivative at zero. The minimisation takes place over nonnegative Stieltjes measures with an integrable cumulative function. Their total mass is free. We first derive the variation of the functional, then use changes of measure which preserve this admissible class. The result will be contact on the *existing* support; the exclusion of gaps comes afterwards. ### 3.1 The moment function before minimisation Fix any $\gamma\in\mathcal U$, without yet assuming that it minimises $\mathcal P$. Compact-strip regularity and Itô's formula give $$ u(t,X_t)=\int_0^t a(s,X_s)\,dB_s,\qquad q(t):=\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2 =\int_0^t\mathbb E a(s,X_s)^2\,ds. $$ The initial term vanishes because zero field makes $\Phi$ even and $u(0,0)=0$. Thus $q(0)=0$, $0\le q(t)\le1$, and $$ q'(t)=\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2\qquad(0\le t<1), $$ with a right derivative at zero. The integrand is continuous on each compact time strip, so $q\in C^1[0,1)$. These facts hold for every admissible coefficient. They do not yet say that $q(t)=t$. The source proves them by smooth approximation on $[0,T]$, $T<1$; it never differentiates the terminal cusp $|x|$ at time one. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][fs-reg]. ### 3.2 The feasible right derivative Let $\eta\in L^1(0,1)$ and suppose that $\gamma+\varepsilon\eta\in\mathcal U$ for $0\le\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$, where $\varepsilon_0>0$. This is a feasibility hypothesis: an arbitrary signed bump in $\gamma$ need not preserve monotonicity. Since $\mathcal U$ is convex, it is enough to check that the endpoint $\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ is admissible. The formula below is the zero-field, $\xi''=1$ specialization of [Chen, Handschy and Lerman, arXiv:1609.04368v4, Proposition 4](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4). Their chord $\gamma_\theta=(1-\theta)\gamma+\theta\gamma_1$ gives this direction by taking $\gamma_1=\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ and $\theta=\varepsilon/\varepsilon_0$. Their class $\mathcal U$ permits unnormalized cumulative measures with finite cumulative integral, so this change of parameter also covers the scaling direction $-\gamma$. We reconstruct the detailed PDE proof from OpenAI's Lemma 6.1. For $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$, put $\beta=\gamma+\varepsilon\eta$, $\widetilde u=\Phi_{\beta,x}$ and $D=\Phi_\beta-\Phi_\gamma$. Subtracting the two PDEs gives $$ D_t=-\frac12D_{xx} -\frac12\beta(\widetilde u+u)D_x -\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\eta u^2. $$ The choice of diffusion $$ dY_t^\varepsilon =\frac12\beta(t)(\widetilde u+u)(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)\,dt+dB_t, \qquad Y_0^\varepsilon=0, $$ cancels the first-order spatial term when Itô's formula is applied to $D(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)$. Its drift has absolute value at most $\beta(t)$, which is integrable. On $[0,T]$ the resulting identity is $$ D(0,0)=\mathbb E D(T,Y_T^\varepsilon) +\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_0^T \eta(t)\mathbb E[u(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)^2]\,dt. $$ At coefficient jumps the time derivatives need only exist almost everywhere. The source obtains this identity by approximating both coefficients by monotone step functions with the same smooth terminal datum, and then passing to the limit using the compact-strip estimates. The control representation, applied with the same control on each side, gives the time-local difference bound $$ \sup_x|D(T,x)|\le\frac{3\varepsilon}{2} \int_T^1|\eta(t)|\,dt. $$ Hence $T\uparrow1$, at fixed $\varepsilon$, removes the terminal term even after division by $\varepsilon$. We obtain the exact finite-change identity $$ \frac{\Phi_{\gamma+\varepsilon\eta}(0,0)-\Phi_\gamma(0,0)} {\varepsilon} =\frac12\int_0^1\eta(t) \mathbb E[u(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)^2]\,dt. $$ As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, the coefficients converge in $L^1$ and have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms. On each fixed strip, their gradients converge uniformly and have common spatial Lipschitz bounds. Coupling with the same Brownian motion and applying Gronwall's inequality therefore gives $Y^\varepsilon\to X$ uniformly on that strip. The integrand converges to $\eta(t)q(t)$ for each $t<1$, and its absolute value is at most $|\eta(t)|$. Dominated convergence, followed by subtraction of the linear Parisi penalty, now yields $$ D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\eta] :=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0} \frac{\mathcal P(\gamma+\varepsilon\eta)-\mathcal P(\gamma)} {\varepsilon} =\frac12\int_0^1\eta(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt. $$ If $\gamma$ is a minimiser, this derivative is nonnegative for every feasible direction. It need not vanish: the minimisation has one-sided constraints. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.1, equations (6.1)–(6.2)][fs-var]. ### 3.3 Which changes of measure are allowed? Write $\mu=\mu_\gamma$ and $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu$, with support relative to $[0,1)$. Tonelli's theorem gives the useful identity $$ \int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt =\int_{[0,1)}\!\int_s^1dt\,\mu(ds) =\int_{[0,1)}(1-s)\,\mu(ds)<\infty. $$ This is weighted finiteness, not a bound on $\mu([0,1))$. In particular, there is no normalisation constraint requiring mass added at one point to be removed elsewhere. Define the tail potential $$ G(s)=\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt\qquad(0\le s<1). $$ It is continuous, satisfies $|G(s)|\le1-s$, and has $G'(s)=s-q(s)$ and $G''(s)=1-q'(s)$ on compact strips, with one-sided interpretations at zero. The following two competitors suffice. | Change to the Stieltjes measure | Direction in the cumulative function | Allowed parameter | Consequence at a minimiser | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Add $\varepsilon\delta_s$, $0\le s<1$ | $\eta(t)=\mathbf1_{[s,1)}(t)$ | $\varepsilon\ge0$ | $G(s)\ge0$ | | Remove $\varepsilon\nu$, where $\nu=\mu|_K$ and $K\subset[0,1)$ is compact | $\eta_K(t)=-\nu([0,t])$ | $0\le\varepsilon\le1$ | $\int_KG(s)\,\mu(ds)\le0$ | For atom addition, the new cumulative function is nonnegative, nondecreasing and right-continuous. Its integral increases by $\varepsilon(1-s)$, so it remains in $\mathcal U$. This includes $s=0$: an atom there adds a constant to $\gamma$ on all of $[0,1)$. The point $1$ is outside the measure's domain and is not an additional competitor. The derivative formula gives $D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\mathbf1_{[s,1)}]=G(s)/2$, proving $G\ge0$ everywhere below one. For removal, choose $T<1$ with $K\subset[0,T]$. Then $\nu(K)\le\gamma(T)<\infty$. The measure $\mu-\varepsilon\nu$ is nonnegative for $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, so its cumulative function is nonnegative, nondecreasing and right-continuous. It lies between zero and $\gamma$, hence is integrable; also $|\eta_K|\le\nu(K)$. Fubini is justified quantitatively by $$ \int_K\!\int_s^1|q(t)-t|\,dt\,\mu(ds) \le\int_K(1-s)\,\mu(ds)\le\nu(K)<\infty. $$ It follows that $$ 0\le D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\eta_K] =-\frac12\int_0^1\nu([0,t])(q(t)-t)\,dt =-\frac12\int_KG(s)\,\mu(ds). $$ Since $G\ge0$, its integral on every compact $K$ is zero. The compact intervals $[0,T]$ exhaust $[0,1)$, so $G=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. If a support point $s$ had $G(s)>0$, continuity would give a relative neighbourhood on which $G$ stays positive. After restricting to a compact interval containing that neighbourhood, the defining property of support would give it positive $\mu$-mass, contradicting the zero integral. Therefore $$ G(s)=0\qquad(s\in S). $$ This step applies to atoms, diffuse mass and singular continuous mass. Removing individual atoms alone would not establish it. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.2][fs-var]. ### 3.4 Contact values and endpoint slopes At $s\in S\cap(0,1)$, the function $G$ has an interior minimum of value zero. Thus $G'(s)=0$ and $G''(s)\ge0$, giving $$ q(s)=s,\qquad q'(s)\le1. $$ If $0\in S$, the argument needs the zero-field initial condition in addition to the one-sided minimum. We have $G(0)=0$ and $q(0)=0$, so $$ G(h)=G(0)+\int_0^h(t-q(t))\,dt =\frac12(1-q'(0))h^2+o(h^2). $$ Nonnegativity for $h>0$ implies $q'(0)\le1$. This works whether or not zero is an atom. The equality $q(0)=0$ comes from symmetry, rather than from differentiating a one-sided minimum. If $0\notin S$, no condition $G(0)=0$ has been obtained or used. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.2][fs-var]. We have now proved, without any no-gap assumption, $$ G\ge0\text{ on }[0,1),\qquad G=0\text{ on }S,\qquad q(s)=s\text{ and }q'(s)\le1\text{ for }s\in S. $$ These are precisely the contact data used in §5. They make no assertion that every zero of $G$ belongs to $S$, or that $q(t)=t$ at a point outside $S$. Terminal, interior and initial gaps remain to be excluded. ### 3.5 What the first-order criterion does, and does not, establish There is also a global alternative to compact mass removal. Atom addition still gives $G\ge0$. Now replace $\mu$ by $(1-\varepsilon)\mu$, or equivalently $\gamma$ by $(1-\varepsilon)\gamma$, for $0\le\varepsilon\le1$. This preserves admissibility, and its direction $-\gamma$ lies in $L^1$, although it may be unbounded. The first variation in §3.2 therefore applies. The signed interchange is justified by $$ \int_{[0,1)}\!\int_s^1|q(t)-t|\,dt\,\mu(ds) =\int_0^1\gamma(t)|q(t)-t|\,dt \le\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty. $$ Consequently $$ 0\le D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[-\gamma] =-\frac12\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu(ds). $$ Together with $G\ge0$, this gives $\int G\,d\mu=0$. Continuity then gives $G=0$ on relative support, including zero, as in §3.3. Finite weighted mass is sufficient throughout; no finite total mass or density of $\mu$ has been assumed. This ordinary argument uses the same integrable-direction first variation as the local removal proof. For the actual moment function associated with $\gamma$, the two potential conditions $G\ge0$ and $G=0$ on $S$ are also sufficient for minimality. This ordinary deduction explains exactly how much variational information has been extracted. For another admissible coefficient $\beta$, let $\nu=\mu_\beta$. The weighted identity above and $|G(s)|\le1-s$ make both measure integrals absolutely convergent, even when either measure has infinite total mass. Fubini gives $$ 2D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\beta-\gamma] =\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\nu(ds) -\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu(ds)\ge0. $$ Here the second integral is zero because $\mu$ is concentrated on its relative support. The control formula also shows that $\mathcal P$ is convex in its coefficient: for a fixed control, the terminal absolute value is convex in the coefficient and both penalties are linear; taking the supremum over the same control class preserves convexity. Therefore $$ \mathcal P(\beta)-\mathcal P(\gamma) \ge D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\beta-\gamma]\ge0. $$ This proves the converse. It agrees with the chord optimality criterion of [Chen, Handschy and Lerman, arXiv:1609.04368v4, Proposition 4, printed p. 14](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4). Chen's zero-temperature treatment obtains the same contact integral by testing $0$ and $2\gamma$ and then using weighted Fubini [Chen (2026), Proposition 3.2, equations (3.11)–(3.12)][chen2026]. The compact-removal proof above keeps the local mass operation explicit. The converse concerns $G$ built from the PDE and diffusion of the same $\gamma$. It does not say that an arbitrary curve with these contact properties comes from a Parisi solution. Nor does it prove full support: the missing input is the strict curvature on an interval where the coefficient is constant, established next. The formal chord statement and the ordinary derivative bridge are distinguished in §12.1.

**Theorem 5.1 (full support).** In the pure zero-field SK model with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ minimize $\mathcal P$. Then $\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1)$ and $\gamma$ is strictly increasing. For every associated diffusion started at zero, $\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2=t$ and $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$ for $0\le t<1$. Keep the same minimiser, diffusion and moment function $q$ throughout. Section 3 has established $G\ge0$, $G=0$ on the support $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma$, and the contact conditions $q(s)=s$, $q'(s)\le1$ at support points. At zero, the value identity comes from symmetry, and the slope bound requires $0\in S$. Section 4 supplies curvature on constant intervals for every admissible coefficient. These premises are available before any support gap is excluded. We first deal with the endpoint at one, then use the curvature estimate on the remaining intervals. For a terminal interval $(a,1)$, including empty support $[0,1)$, the cusp estimate gives $1-q(t)\gtrsim\sqrt{1-t}$ and hence $G<0$ near one. On a positive plateau with two contact endpoints, strict convexity puts $q'$ below its endpoint chord, although its integral must equal the interval length. On a zero plateau the heat argument makes $q'$ strictly increasing, below the right contact slope. At an initial gap, use the one-sided contact slope if $0\in S$; otherwise the coefficient is zero and symmetry supplies $q(0)=0$. **Why a terminal plateau violates the variational inequality.** Suppose that $\gamma=c$ on $(a,1)$, where $0\le a<1$ and $c\ge0$ is finite. The endpoint $1$ is outside the support domain, so there is no contact condition there to complete an endpoint-chord argument. Instead we will prove $$ 1-q(t)\ge C\sqrt{1-t} \tag{5.1} $$ for some $C>0$ and every $t$ sufficiently close to one. The proof separates two facts: the diffusion puts positive probability density near zero, and the smoothed terminal slope has a definite deficit from $\pm1$ in a shrinking window around zero. Fix $s\in(a,1)$ and let $\rho_s$ be the law of $X_s$. Choose $R<\infty$ such that $p_0=\rho_s([-R,R])>0$. For $c>0$, set $$ h(t,y)=\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt{1-t}Z|},\qquad \Phi(t,y)=c^{-1}\log h(t,y), $$ where $Z$ is standard normal. The drift on this interval is $c\Phi_x=h_x/h$, and the transition density is $$ k_{s,t}(x,y)=p_{t-s}(y-x)\frac{h(t,y)}{h(s,x)},\qquad p_v(z)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/(2v)}. \tag{5.2} $$ The heat-semigroup identity normalises this kernel; equivalently, for Brownian motion started at $(s,x)$, $h(t,B_t)/h(s,x)$ is the positive mean-one change of measure which adds the drift $h_x/h$. For $c=0$, the same kernel formula applies with $h=1$, and the value function is the ordinary heat evolution of $|x|$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3, proof of (6.6)][fs-var]. Put $L=1-s$ and $\delta=L/2$. For $s+\delta\le t<1$, $|x|\le R$ and $|y|\le1$, $$ p_{t-s}(y-x)\ge (2\pi L)^{-1/2}e^{-(R+1)^2/(2\delta)}=:k_*>0, $$ while $h(t,y)\ge1$ and $h(s,x)\le e^{cR}\mathbb E e^{c\sqrt L|Z|}=:M<\infty$. Integrating (5.2) over the part of $\rho_s$ in $[-R,R]$ therefore gives a density $f_t$ of $X_t$ with $$ f_t(y)\ge p_0k_*/M=:m>0 \quad(s+\delta\le t<1,\ |y|\le1). \tag{5.3} $$ Only positive mass of a compact set was needed at time $s$; no density assumption on $\rho_s$ has entered. Now write $\varepsilon=1-t$ and restrict to $|y|\le\sqrt\varepsilon$. Differentiating the terminal heat formula gives, with the unweighted interpretation for $c=0$, $$ u(t,y)= \frac{\mathbb E[\operatorname{sgn}(y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z) e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}]} {\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}}. $$ The denominator is at most $D=e^c\mathbb E e^{c|Z|}<\infty$. Each sign has unnormalised mass at least $p_*:=\mathbb P(Z\ge1)>0$: the threshold $|y/\sqrt\varepsilon|$ is at most one, and the exponential weight is at least one. Hence each sign has tilted probability at least $\theta=p_*/D\in(0,1/2)$. It follows that $$ |u(t,y)|\le1-2\theta,\qquad 1-u(t,y)^2\ge4\theta(1-\theta)=:\kappa>0. $$ Multiplying this uniform deficit by the density lower bound (5.3) and the window width $2\sqrt\varepsilon$ yields $$ 1-q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}(1-u(t,y)^2)f_t(y)\,dy \ge 2m\kappa\sqrt{1-t}. $$ This proves (5.1) with $C=2m\kappa$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3, density and terminal-window estimates][fs-var]. The sign of the contradiction is now explicit. For $s'$ sufficiently close to one, the estimate holds at every $t\in[s',1)$, so $$ \begin{aligned} G(s')&=\int_{s'}^1(q(t)-t)\,dt\\ &\le\frac{(1-s')^2}{2} -\frac{2C}{3}(1-s')^{3/2}<0. \end{aligned} $$ The final inequality holds once $\sqrt{1-s'}<4C/3$. It contradicts the nonnegative cost of adding an atom at $s'$. This proof covers $c=0$ as well as $c>0$. In particular, empty support is impossible: then $\mu_\gamma=0$ and $\gamma=0$ on all of $[0,1)$. The terminal-plateau conclusion was already recorded in [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Remark 7][acz]; the estimates above supply the quantitative argument needed here. **A shorter qualitative exclusion.** The existing curvature input also excludes a terminal support gap without estimating its boundary layer. Contact gives $$ q(a)=a,\qquad q(b)=b,\qquad q'(a),q'(b)\le1. \tag{5.4} $$ If the constant coefficient is $c>0$, Section 4 makes $q'$ strictly convex in the gap. Continuity extends the chord comparison to its endpoints, giving $$ q'(t)<\frac{b-t}{b-a}q'(a)+\frac{t-a}{b-a}q'(b)\le1, \qquad a0. $$ The first term is nonnegative; strict convexity makes the second positive. Only continuity of $q'$ is needed at the ends. For example, a jump $\Delta\gamma$ at $s$ gives the one-sided identity $$ q''(s+)-q''(s-)=-2\Delta\gamma\,\mathbb E a(s,X_s)^3. $$ It follows by applying Itô's formula to $a^2$ and using continuity of its derivative moments on a compact strip. Taking $\gamma=0$ before $s=1/2$ and $\gamma=1/2$ afterward makes this jump strictly negative; the terminal Cole–Hopf solution has positive Hessian. If $(0,b)$ is a gap and $0\in S$, the preceding proof applies using the one-sided contact slope bound at zero. Because $(0,b)$ contains no mass, the support condition at zero forces an atom there and hence $c=\gamma(0)>0$. Its absence has not been proved at this stage. If instead the complementary component is $[0,b)$ with $0\notin S$, there is no mass anywhere in $[0,b)$. Thus $\gamma=0$ there. The identity $q(0)=0$ comes from zero-field symmetry, and the right endpoint gives $q(b)=b$, $q'(b)\le1$. Here $q''(t)>0$ for $00 \qquad(0\le a0$ is already impossible: either $h\le1$ everywhere, forcing $h\equiv1$ by its integral, or it attains an interior maximum above one, where $h'=0$ and $h''\le0$. This is an elementary deduction from these premises. Chen's conditional crossing theorem, with its own hypotheses, is of this form; §4 proves the stronger $q'''>0$ throughout a positive plateau, without a minimizer premise. See [Chen, arXiv:2607.18032v1, Proposition 4.2 and the proof of Proposition 4.3][chen26]. Neither statement supplies terminal contact at the excluded endpoint one.

**Proposition 6.1 (terminal value).** For the minimizer and diffusion of
Theorem 5.1 there is a spin-valued terminal variable $U_1$ such that
$u(t,X_t)=\mathbb E[U_1\mid\mathcal F_t]$ and
$$
P_*=\mathbb E[U_1B_1]=\int_0^1\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt.
\tag{6.1}
$$
Its finite-cutoff tail lies in $[0,1-T]$. This proposition uses the
attained Parisi formula in addition to the support theorem.

The bounded martingale $u(t,X_t)$ converges almost surely and in $L^2$
to $U_1$. Its second moment tends to one because $q(t)=t$.
Since $|U_1|\le1$, $\mathbb E U_1^2=1$ forces $U_1^2=1$ almost surely.
Uniform integrability identifies $u(t,X_t)=\mathbb E[U_1\mid\mathcal F_t]$,
which is the conditional-expectation identity used below.

The drift bound $|\gamma u|\le\gamma\in L^1$ gives convergence of $X_t$
to $X_1$. Uniform terminal convergence of $\Phi$ to $|x|$, together
with convexity, gives $u(t,x_t)\to\operatorname{sgn}(x)$ when
$x_t\to x\ne0$. Thus $U_1X_1=|X_1|$, including when $X_1=0$;
no proof that this event has probability zero is needed.

Itô's formula gives
$$
\mathbb E\Phi(t,X_t)=\Phi(0,0)+\frac12\int_0^t\gamma(s)s\,ds.
$$
The terminal limit first gives
$\Phi(0,0)=\mathbb E|X_1|-\tfrac12\int_0^1s\gamma(s)ds$.
Subtracting the second half from the definition of the functional yields
$\mathcal P(\gamma)=\mathbb E|X_1|-\int_0^1s\gamma(s)\,ds$.
The ground-state Parisi formula identifies this with $P_*$.
The diffusion equation, conditional expectation and Fubini give
$$
\mathbb E[U_1X_1]=\mathbb E[U_1B_1]
 +\int_0^1\gamma(s)\mathbb E[u(s,X_s)^2]\,ds.
$$
Bounded $u,U_1$ and integrable $\gamma$ justify these terms.
Combining the identities and using stochastic integral covariance gives
$$
P_*=\mathbb E|X_1|-\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt
 =\mathbb E[U_1B_1]=\int_0^1\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt.
$$
The last integral is absolutely bounded by one because
$\mathbb E|a|\le(\mathbb E a^2)^{1/2}=1$.
Full support supplies $\mathbb E a^2=1$, whereas the value uses
$\int\mathbb E a$. Substituting the second moment into the value identity

## 4. The full-support theorem

**Source theorem ([OpenAI (2026a), Theorem 1.1][support-manuscript]).**
In the pure, zero-field model with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, let $\gamma$ be an
admissible integrable minimiser of $\mathcal P$. Its Stieltjes measure
has full relative support on $[0,1)$, and $\gamma$ is strictly increasing.
For every associated diffusion and every $0\le t<1$,

$$
\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2]=t,\qquad
\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2]=1.
$$

The cumulative function determines its measure uniquely; for a fixed
Brownian motion the associated diffusion is unique by the cited
regularity results. The theorem requires a minimiser,
not merely an admissible candidate. Zero field supplies $q(0)=0$;
$\xi''=1$ enters the curvature estimate. The statement does not cover
nonzero field or general mixed-spin covariance functions.

## 5. Why a flat interval cannot minimise

### 5.1 Allowed changes and their first-order cost

The **first variation** in a direction $\eta$ is the derivative at
zero of $\varepsilon\mapsto\mathcal P(\gamma+\varepsilon\eta)$.
At a minimum its right derivative is nonnegative whenever small
$\varepsilon\ge0$ leave the candidate admissible. It need not vanish:
the opposite change may violate nonnegativity or monotonicity.
Precisely, let $\eta\in L^1(0,1)$, meaning $\int_0^1|\eta(t)|\,dt<\infty$, and suppose
$\gamma+\varepsilon\eta$ stays admissible for every
$0\le\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$, for some $\varepsilon_0>0$.
The formula is

$$
D\mathcal P(\gamma)[\eta]
=\frac12\int_0^1\eta(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt.
$$

Here $q$ belongs to the unperturbed candidate $\gamma$.
The term $-t/2$ comes from the explicit penalty in $\mathcal P$;
$q(t)/2$ is the sensitivity of the reoptimised control value. The latter
is the analytic content of the formula, not differentiation with a fixed
control. [Chen–Handschy–Lerman (2018), Proposition 4][chl-optimality]
gives the derivative along the segment joining any two admissible
coefficients. Taking the second endpoint to be
$\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ and rescaling the segment parameter gives
the formula above. The detailed proof in
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.1][support-variation] compares value functions
and bounds the terminal remainder by the $L^1$ tail of $\eta$.

Adding a small atom at scale $s$ raises the cumulative function at
*every* later scale. It is always allowed: the total mass is not
fixed, so no compensating removal is required. Its direction is
$\eta(t)=\mathbf1_{[s,1)}(t)$, equal to zero before $s$ and one
from $s$ onward. Thus

$$
D\mathcal P(\gamma)[\mathbf1_{[s,1)}]
=\frac12\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt=:\frac12G(s).
$$

For the candidate in Figure 1, adding $\varepsilon$ mass at $s=1/2$
creates a jump of height $\varepsilon$ there and raises the entire
remaining curve by $\varepsilon$. The coefficient changes only on
that tail, but its optimised value and feedback must be recomputed:
earlier starting states also face a changed future control problem. The
first-variation theorem accounts for this dependence. Its formula
has a tail integral because that is where the coefficient changes:
$G(s)/2$ is the marginal cost of placing mass at $s$. At a minimiser,
$G(s)\ge0$ for every $s<1$.

For the two weights in Section 2, the same accounting gives

$$
\int_0^1\gamma(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt
=2G(1/4)+G(3/4).
$$

Each weight is charged for its entire remaining tail. The $q$ and $G$
in this identity belong to that candidate; no optimality has been assumed.
Reducing both weights by a fraction $\varepsilon$ multiplies the
cumulative function by $1-\varepsilon$.

Suppose temporarily that this two-weight candidate minimised
$\mathcal P$. Addition would give two nonnegative costs,
$G(1/4)\ge0$ and $G(3/4)\ge0$, while the allowed reduction would give

$$
0\le-\frac12\bigl(2G(1/4)+G(3/4)\bigr).
$$

Both costs must be zero: their positive-weighted sum is nonnegative,
and the reduction forces it to be nonpositive. This is a necessary
condition under the temporary minimiser assumption, not a claim that
the two-weight candidate attains the minimum.

For a general minimiser, the same argument replaces the finite sum by
an integral. The direction $\eta=-\gamma$
is integrable, and $(1-\varepsilon)\gamma$ remains admissible for
$0\le\varepsilon\le1$. It scales all existing mass by the same
factor. For the continuous candidate in Figure 1, it multiplies the
two nonzero slopes and the plateau height by $1-\varepsilon$;
it works for diffuse mass as well as atoms.
The weighted-sum identity becomes

$$
0\le D\mathcal P(\gamma)[-\gamma]
=-\frac12\int_0^1\gamma(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt
=-\frac12\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu_\gamma(ds).
$$

The exchange of integration order is valid even if the total mass is
infinite. Its absolute integral is bounded by the area from Section 2:

$$
\int_{[0,1)}\int_s^1|q(t)-t|\,dt\,\mu_\gamma(ds)
=\int_0^1\gamma(t)|q(t)-t|\,dt
\le\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty.
$$

Since $G\ge0$, its integral must be zero. If $G$ were positive at a
support point, continuity would bound it below by a positive number
on a neighbourhood carrying positive mass, contradicting that zero
integral. Hence $G=0$ on the support. This is **contact**: the
nonnegative function touches zero there. The scaling argument is the
variational argument of [Chen, Proposition 3.2, equations (3.11)–(3.12)][chen-support],
applied with the integrable-direction formula above.

Scaling removes only mass that exists. In Figure 1, even the supported
point $1/4$ has no atom: intervals around it carry mass, but the point
itself does not. Subtracting $\varepsilon\delta_{1/4}$ would create a
downward jump. For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$ the cumulative values would
remain nonnegative, but the function would no longer be nondecreasing.
Support alone does not permit atom removal. We have proved contact
on the support, not that every zero of $G$ must carry mass.

### 5.2 Contact gives endpoint conditions

We need information about $q$ at the ends of a possible gap. An interior
support point $s$ is a minimum of $G$. Since
$G'(s)=s-q(s)$ and $G''(s)=1-q'(s)$, ordinary calculus gives

$$
q(s)=s,\qquad q'(s)\le1.
$$

At zero, if it belongs to the support, contact and symmetry give
$G(0)=q(0)=0$. If $q'(0)>1$, continuity would give $q'(t)>1$
for small positive $t$. Integration would then give $q(t)>t$, so
$G'(t)=t-q(t)<0$. Starting from $G(0)=0$, this would force $G(t)<0$,
a contradiction. Hence $q'(0)\le1$. This one-sided argument includes
an atom at zero.

### 5.3 Strict curvature creates an impossible integral

The support is relatively closed in $[0,1)$. Starting at a missing
point, enlarge its mass-free interval until it reaches support or a
boundary of the domain. Such a maximal interval has two
support endpoints, starts at zero outside the support, or reaches one.
We treat these three cases in order; the last includes empty support.

First suppose $(r,s)$ has both endpoints in the support, with
$0\le r<s<1$. Its constant height $c$ is necessarily positive:
for $t$ inside the gap, a small relative neighbourhood of $r$ lies in
$[0,t]$ and has positive mass, so $c=\mu_\gamma([0,t])>0$.
If $r=0$, this mass is an atom at zero. Contact imposes

$$
q(r)=r,\quad q(s)=s,\quad q'(r)\le1,\quad q'(s)\le1.
$$

The first two conditions require area $s-r$ under $q'$ across the gap.
A calculus model shows how strict convexity can prevent this. On the
earlier interval $[1/3,2/3]$, put $x=3t-1$ and consider the slope
$1-x(1-x)$. Its endpoints equal one, but

$$
\int_{1/3}^{2/3}[1-(3t-1)(2-3t)]\,dt
=\frac13\int_0^1[1-x(1-x)]\,dx=\frac5{18}.
$$

The missing area is $1/3-5/18=1/18$. This is a calculus model, not a
computed SK moment curve. The next input forces the actual $q'$ below
its endpoint chord in the same way.

**Strict-curvature input ([OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][support-curvature]).**
For any admissible coefficient equal to $c>0$ on an open interval,
its moment curve satisfies, strictly inside that interval,

$$
q'''(t)\ge\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0
\qquad(r<t<s).
$$

Section 7.3 explains how this sign is obtained after expectation.
The gap argument uses its strict sign; it does not use the particular
number $1/1000$.
The final inequality uses $a(t,x)>0$, proved by Gaussian smoothing
on the constant interval ([OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][support-regularity]);
convexity of $\Phi$ alone would only give $a\ge0$.
Because $q'''=(q')''$, the function $q'$ is strictly convex: between
two points its graph lies strictly below their joining chord.
The moment identity makes $q'$ continuous at the endpoints, even if
$\gamma$ jumps there; higher derivatives are needed only inside the gap.
Hence

$$
q'(t)<\frac{s-t}{s-r}q'(r)+\frac{t-r}{s-r}q'(s)\le1
\qquad(r<t<s).
$$

### 7.1 Why the zero candidate does not minimise

Return to the Gaussian value and slope from Section 3. With $\gamma=0$,

$$

\qquad

A Gaussian integral gives

$$

$$

=\frac12\int_0^1\left(\frac2\pi\arcsin t-t\right)dt
